summary: Sets out requirements for how Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) signaling should be used and extended to support Automatically Switched Optical Networks (ASON). It focuses on time-division multiplexed connections such as SONET/SDH and optical transport networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies run big glass-fiber networks and want them to set up connections on their own. This memo lists what the control software must be able to do to make that work.

questions: what is ason in optical networks
what is a soft permanent connection
subtitle: What GMPLS signaling must do to control automatically switched optical networks: calls, soft connections, restart, crankback and more.

tldr.problem: GMPLS signaling can set up TDM connections such as SONET/SDH and OTN, but the ITU-T ASON architecture needs capabilities it does not yet provide.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the needed functions: soft permanent connections, call and connection separation, call segments, extended restart, extended label association, crankback and additional error cases. It also requires any extensions to be backward compatible.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document only. It defines no protocol messages, and the actual extensions are left to other documents.

today: RFC 4139 is an Informational requirements document and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no protocol itself; the signaling specifications it builds on are RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

sections.title: Scope and Problem Statement
sections.content:
The Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) protocols control different switching technologies, including Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) connections such as SONET/SDH and Optical Transport Networks. The ITU-T defines the architecture of an Automatically Switched Optical Network (ASON) in G.8080, which needs generic capabilities such as call and connection separation, plus more specific ones such as soft permanent connections.

This RFC covers only the signaling side, building on the GMPLS signaling specifications RFC 3471 and RFC 3473. ASON distinguishes three reference points: the user-network interface (UNI), the external network-network interface (E-NNI) between control domains, and the internal NNI (I-NNI) within a domain. The RFC does not restrict which protocols are used at those interfaces, and interworking with non-GMPLS protocols is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Big telephone-style networks want to wire up their own connections automatically. This memo says what the wiring-instructions language needs to be able to say.

sections.title: Soft Permanent Connections and Calls
sections.content:
A soft permanent connection (SPC) joins a permanent connection on the source user side, a permanent connection on the destination user side, and a switched connection across the network. A management system typically asks the ingress node to set up the switched part using GMPLS signaling. Signaling MUST be able to indicate the outgoing link and label for the destination provisioned connection, and SHOULD also indicate the requested service level.

ASON also separates a call, an association between endpoints that supports a service, from the connections that carry traffic. A call can have zero, one or many connections, each set up and released with its own signaling messages. GMPLS signaling SHOULD include a call identification mechanism and allow end-to-end call capability exchange. When a call crosses several control domains it MAY be split into call segments, each with its own connections and policies.
sections.plainLanguage: A call is like agreeing to talk, and a connection is the actual phone line. You can agree first, and later open one line, several lines, or none.

sections.title: Restart, Crankback and Errors
sections.content:
Extended restart. A control plane failure MUST NOT release established calls and connections. After recovery the control entity MUST be able to recover call and connection status, neighbor connectivity, and the association between each call and its connections. Setups still pending SHOULD be released or continued, while releases in progress MUST complete.

Crankback. When setup fails because a link or node is blocked, the request can be retried on an alternate path. The blocking resource MUST be identified in the error response sent to a repair node, which computes a detour and restarts setup. The path computer SHOULD remember all blockages seen, and retries SHOULD be strictly limited per connection or per node, ending with a "Maximum number of re-routings exceeded" error sent upstream.

Additional error cases cover call and SPC mistakes (such as wrong call IDs or invalid interface IDs), policy failures, and a wrongly specified service level.
sections.plainLanguage: If the controller crashes, calls already running must keep going. If a road is blocked while setting up a line, the network backs up, tries another road, and eventually gives up instead of trying forever.

sections.title: Extended Label Association
sections.content:
In GMPLS a label identifies the resource used on a link for one connection, such as a timeslot, wavelength or port. In ASON, a label value may not be consistent across a link. The RFC's example has GMPLS nodes A and Z interconnected across non-GMPLS SONET/SDH nodes B and C. Node A's outgoing timeslot with label [1,0,0,0,0] may be rearranged into timeslot #6 by B and #4 by C, so by the time Z sees label [1,0,0,0,0] it no longer matches Z's local timeslot.

So a label association mechanism SHOULD map the received remote label to a locally significant one. The mapping can come from manual provisioning or from discovery, and either MAY be used. For directly connected TDM interfaces no mapping is needed, because the label structure is implicit and the mapping is one-to-one.
sections.plainLanguage: If two friends number the seats on a bus differently, seat 1 for one may be seat 6 for the other. A translation table fixes the mix-up.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Any extension to GMPLS signaling made for these requirements MUST be backward compatible. In a network where some nodes support the extensions and some do not, it MUST still be possible to set up conventional RFC 3473 connections between any pair of nodes and across any set of nodes. New calls and connections MUST NOT perturb existing ones.

Transit nodes that do not need the new functions MUST be able to pass setup information onward unmodified. A node that is asked for a function it lacks MUST be able to reject it using existing GMPLS mechanisms without harming the network.
sections.plainLanguage: New features must not break old machines. Old machines should either pass messages along or politely say no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that, per G.8080, a connection cannot be established before call setup completes, and policy and authentication are applied before the call is established. It states that the document introduces no new security requirements to GMPLS signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: You must be allowed in before a line is opened, and this memo adds no new safety rules.

viz.caption: THE SEVEN ASON FUNCTIONS GMPLS SIGNALING MUST SUPPORT

items.title: Soft permanent connection
items.text: Switched part set up between provisioned user links.

items.title: Call and connection separation
items.text: A call is a service relationship; connections carry traffic.

items.title: Call segments
items.text: A call split across control domains.

items.title: Extended restart
items.text: Control plane failures do not release established calls.

items.title: Extended label association
items.text: Map remote labels to local ones.

items.title: Crankback
items.text: Retry setup on a detour around a blocked resource.
